description: Layer 1 native-agent architectural review across code, configuration, and architecture over the ten mandatory security categories of the calcom-monorepo. Detection/reporting only: every recommendation is advisory and was NOT applied, and no source file was modified. Findings are anchored to concrete file:line locations and, where possible, corroborated by the deterministic Layer 2 (Semgrep) and Layer 3a (sink-inventory) artifacts.

categories.summary: Assessed the legacy AES-256-CBC path (unauthenticated, raw Latin1 key, random IV) against the modern authenticated AES-256-GCM keyring. Residual risk is concentrated in the unauthenticated CBC format and raw-key handling, both retained under the encryption-key-continuity hard constraint.

Reviewed NextAuth providers/JWT, bcryptjs password verification, the v2 four/five-credential api-auth strategy, ~15 authorization guard folders, PBAC, and the TOTP routes (which require an authenticated session plus password re-verification). Residual risk is an over-long magic-link TTL and the inherent non-revocability of stateless JWT sessions.

Evaluated edge middleware (CSP nonce, cookie clearance, return-to redirect), the CSP generator (dev unsafe-inline/eval vs prod nonce+strict-dynamic), NestJS helmet/CORS/ValidationPipe bootstrap, and rate-limit IP derivation. Residual risk: CSP enforced only on login routes, cf-connecting-ip trust, and a cookie-driven open-redirect surface.

Surveyed the v1 next-api-middleware chain (request-id, error capture, pagination, auth, rate-limit) and the file-based route layout. Residual risk stems from the opt-in nature of the middleware and the broad request-derived log-injection surface.

Inspected the multi-stage Dockerfile (default build secrets, root user, HEALTHCHECK), the local-dev compose stack, and a representative subset of the 59 GitHub Actions workflows. Residual risk: predictable build-time secret defaults, root container user, run-step shell injection, and pull_request_target workflows that check out PR-controlled refs.

Examined outbound HMAC-SHA256 signing (with an unsigned no-secret fallback), inbound Vercel HMAC-SHA1 verification, and app-store payment webhook verifiers. Residual risk: subscribers may receive unsigned deliveries and the Vercel path uses SHA-1, while btcpay/vercel both use constant-time comparison.

Compared the v2 global ValidationPipe whitelist against v1's per-route Zod validation and boundary safeParse usage. Residual risk is the enforcement asymmetry between the two APIs and any unguarded parse boundary contributing to the type-confusion surface.

Traced the parent/iframe handshake and postMessage flows (init, SDK events, command dispatch). Residual risk: parent-to-iframe messages use a wildcard targetOrigin and the inbound parent listener dispatches actions without validating event.origin, both bounded to non-sensitive UI commands.

Contrasted the legacy v1 middleware chain (query-parameter API key, per-route opt-in, per-user rate limit) with the v2 NestJS guard chain (header bearer, global guards, per-credential limits). Residual risk is enforcement and transport divergence rather than absence of controls on either side.

Reviewed Next.js configuration (poweredByHeader:false), committed env templates, the App Router cron-auth pattern, and React HTML-injection sinks. Residual risk: a publicly-committed CRON_API_KEY default protecting sensitive cron routes, non-constant-time cron-secret comparison, and a dangerouslySetInnerHTML surface to verify.

findings.title: Legacy symmetric encryption uses unauthenticated AES-256-CBC
findings.description: symmetricEncrypt/symmetricDecrypt use ALGORITHM="aes256" (Node alias for AES-256-CBC), an unauthenticated cipher mode. CBC ciphertext is malleable and provides no integrity, exposing the legacy credential-encryption path to bit-flipping and padding-oracle style attacks if ciphertext is ever attacker-influenced. No MAC/auth tag accompanies the ciphertext format `iv:ciphertext`.
findings.recommendation: Prefer the authenticated AES-256-GCM keyring (packages/lib/crypto/keyring.ts) for all new secrets and plan a backward-compatible migration of legacy CBC values; do not change the in-use key or format in this audit.
findings.demotionReason: A random per-message IV is generated (packages/lib/crypto.ts:17) and the modern authenticated AES-256-GCM keyring already exists for new secrets; the legacy CBC path is retained under the platform's encryption-key-continuity hard constraint and is not directly fed attacker-controlled ciphertext.

findings.title: Encryption key consumed as a raw Latin1 buffer without a key-derivation function
findings.description: The key is materialized with Buffer.from(key, "latin1") in both symmetricEncrypt (line 16) and symmetricDecrypt (line 32). CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is therefore used verbatim as raw key bytes with no KDF (PBKDF2/HKDF/scrypt) and no salt; key strength depends entirely on operator-supplied entropy, and Latin1 decoding silently truncates/maps multibyte input rather than rejecting an out-of-spec key length.
findings.recommendation: Derive a fixed-length key via HKDF/scrypt from the configured secret and validate key length at startup; keep the current key value unchanged (encryption-key continuity is a hard constraint).
findings.demotionReason: Deployment docs require a 32-byte CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY and the newer keyring validates key length explicitly (packages/lib/crypto/keyring.ts:67-70, base64url 32-byte keys); the value cannot be rotated in this detection-only engagement.

findings.title: AES-256-GCM decryption omits explicit authTagLength hardening
findings.description: createDecipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, nonce) is called without the { authTagLength: 16 } option. While the auth tag is still validated via setAuthTag, not pinning the tag length is a defense-in-depth gap that a truncated-tag forgery attempt could probe.
findings.recommendation: Pass { authTagLength: 16 } to createDecipheriv (and createCipheriv) to pin GCM tag length explicitly.
findings.demotionReason: GCM remains authenticated and the 16-byte tag produced by getAuthTag is enforced via setAuthTag; the default tag length already matches, so exposure is theoretical.

findings.title: Magic-link email token lifetime is 10 hours despite a comment stating 10 minutes
findings.description: The NextAuth EmailProvider sets maxAge: 10 * 60 * 60 (36000 seconds = 10 hours) while the adjacent comment reads "Magic links are valid for 10 min only". The effective passwordless sign-in window is two orders of magnitude larger than intended, widening the interception/replay window for emailed verification links.
findings.recommendation: Align the maxAge with the documented intent (e.g. 10 * 60 for 10 minutes) and add a test asserting the magic-link TTL.
findings.demotionReason: Verification tokens are single-use and bound to email delivery, and NextAuth invalidates the token on first successful use; the issue is an over-long lifetime rather than a missing control.

findings.title: Stateless JWT sessions have no server-side revocation; logout only deletes the cookie
findings.description: session.strategy is "jwt", so sessions are stateless bearer tokens. Logout deletes the next-auth.session-token cookie at the edge (apps/web/proxy.ts:101) but a previously issued JWT remains valid until expiry, so a captured token cannot be centrally revoked before maxAge elapses.
findings.recommendation: Consider short JWT lifetimes plus a server-side denylist or rotating session version claim for high-assurance logout/force-revocation flows.
findings.demotionReason: Per-user sessionTimeout shortens maxAge during JWT encode (packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:527) and cookies are issued Secure/HttpOnly via defaultCookies(https) (line 534); stateless JWT is an intentional, widely accepted NextAuth design.

findings.title: Enforced Content-Security-Policy is applied only to login routes
findings.description: shouldEnforceCsp returns true only for paths starting with /auth/login or /login (apps/web/proxy.ts:64-66). Because getCspHeader emits no header when enforcement is off (apps/web/lib/csp.ts:44-51), the nonce-based CSP that mitigates XSS is absent on the vast majority of authenticated application pages.
findings.recommendation: Roll out the nonce-based enforced CSP across all app routes (not just login) once streaming-script nonce coverage is complete; until then, track the gap explicitly.
findings.demotionReason: A nonce + strict-dynamic CSP is fully implemented for the highest-risk credential-entry pages, and React's default output escaping plus server-side input validation provide baseline XSS defense elsewhere.

findings.title: Development CSP enables 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval'
findings.description: In the non-production branch, script-src resolves to "'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' https: http:", disabling script-source restrictions during development.
findings.recommendation: Keep the relaxed policy strictly behind the IS_PRODUCTION guard (as implemented) and avoid shipping any build that evaluates the dev branch.
findings.demotionReason: The relaxed directives are gated by IS_PRODUCTION; production uses 'nonce-<n>' 'strict-dynamic' (apps/web/lib/csp.ts:22), so the weakness does not reach production traffic.

findings.title: style-src permits 'unsafe-inline' in non-strict and development policies
findings.description: style-src includes 'unsafe-inline' whenever CSP_POLICY="non-strict" or in development, allowing inline style injection (a lower-impact CSS-based vector) on those configurations.
findings.recommendation: Adopt nonces/hashes for inline styles so 'unsafe-inline' can be removed from style-src even in non-strict mode.
findings.demotionReason: Default production policy omits 'unsafe-inline' for style-src (empty string at line 30), and CSS injection carries materially lower impact than script injection.

findings.title: Rate-limit IP derivation trusts the client-supplied cf-connecting-ip header first
findings.description: Both handleRequest (line 57) and getTracker (line 215) resolve the client IP as request.headers["cf-connecting-ip"] ?? request.headers["CF-Connecting-IP"] ?? request.ip. If the API is reachable without strictly terminating behind Cloudflare, a client can spoof cf-connecting-ip to rotate its rate-limit identity and bypass IP-based throttling.
findings.recommendation: Only trust cf-connecting-ip when the connecting peer is a verified Cloudflare egress IP; otherwise fall back to the socket address (request.ip).
findings.demotionReason: Authenticated requests are tracked by SHA-256 hash of the API key / access token / OAuth client BEFORE the IP fallback (apps/api/v2/src/lib/throttler-guard.ts:217-228), so IP spoofing only affects anonymous traffic; the canonical deployment fronts the API with Cloudflare.

findings.title: Open-redirect surface: edge middleware redirects to an unvalidated return-to cookie
findings.description: On /apps/installed the middleware reads the return-to cookie and issues NextResponse.redirect(new URL(returnTo.value, req.url)). Because new URL() honours an absolute URL in the first argument, a return-to value such as https://evil.example overrides the base origin, yielding an open redirect if the cookie can be planted (e.g. via an earlier injection or subdomain).
findings.recommendation: Validate that the resolved redirect target is same-origin (or matches an allowlist) before redirecting; reject or strip absolute external URLs.
findings.demotionReason: The redirect target comes from a cookie rather than a directly attacker-supplied query parameter, requiring a prior write primitive, and the cookie is deleted immediately after use (apps/web/proxy.ts:89).

findings.title: API v1 security middleware is opt-in per route rather than globally enforced
findings.description: The legacy API composes auth and throttling through next-api-middleware labels (middlewareOrder: extendRequest, captureErrors, verifyApiKey, rateLimitApiKey, addRequestId, captureUserId) that each route must explicitly apply. Across ~82 file-based handlers, any route that forgets to wrap itself with verifyApiKey/rateLimitApiKey ships unauthenticated or unthrottled, with no framework-level backstop.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a default-deny wrapper or lint/test that asserts every public v1 route applies the auth + rate-limit middleware chain.
findings.demotionReason: A shared withMiddleware helper standardizes ordering and is consistently applied across the v1 route set, and verifyApiKey + rateLimitApiKey unit tests exist alongside the helpers.

findings.title: Broad log-injection surface from request-derived values written to logs
findings.description: Request handling logs request-derived context across the API and packages; unsanitized user-controlled values flowing into log lines enable log forging/injection (CRLF, fake entries) and can poison downstream log analysis. This is an architecture-wide observation seeded by the Layer 3a inventory rather than a single line.
findings.recommendation: Centralize logging through a structured logger that encodes/escapes user-controlled fields and strips CR/LF before emission.
findings.demotionReason: Logging is funneled through structured logger utilities and request-id correlation (addRequestid.ts), limiting free-form string concatenation; impact is integrity-of-logs rather than direct code execution.

findings.title: Dockerfile defines default build-time secret values for auth and encryption keys
findings.description: ARG NEXTAUTH_SECRET=secret (line 11) and ARG CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY=secret (line 12) provide weak default values that are promoted into ENV (lines 29-30) and consumed by the Next.js build. If an image is built without overriding these args, the resulting artifact is associated with the predictable value "secret", and the defaults invite copy-paste into real deployments.
findings.recommendation: Remove the insecure defaults and fail the build when NEXTAUTH_SECRET / CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY are unset, forcing explicit secure values; inject real secrets only at runtime.
findings.demotionReason: These are build-time ARGs needed for the Next.js compile step rather than runtime secrets; production deployments inject real values at runtime (docker-compose passes them through, and start.sh re-templates), so the default does not necessarily reach a running instance.

findings.title: Container image runs as root (no USER directive)
findings.description: None of the build/runner stages declare a USER, so the final image starts the application as root (CMD scripts/start.sh at line 94). A container compromise therefore begins with root in the container, increasing blast radius if combined with a kernel or runtime escape.
findings.recommendation: Create and switch to a non-root user (USER node) for the runner stage and ensure file ownership/permissions are compatible.
findings.demotionReason: Production orchestration commonly enforces runAsNonRoot/securityContext at the platform layer, and a HEALTHCHECK is defined (Dockerfile:91-92); this is a hardening gap rather than an exploitable flaw on its own.

findings.title: GitHub Actions workflows contain shell-injection-prone run steps
findings.description: Semgrep flags run: steps that interpolate context expressions directly into the shell across three locations (release-docker.yaml:53, cubic-devin-review-trigger.yml:18, actions/docker-build-and-test/action.yml:121). Untrusted interpolated values (e.g. PR-derived fields) embedded in run scripts can lead to command injection in CI with access to repository secrets.
findings.recommendation: Move interpolated values into env: bindings and reference them as "$VAR" in run steps; never inline ${{ github.event.* }} directly into shell commands.
findings.demotionReason: Exploitation requires an interpolated value to be attacker-controllable for the specific step; several occurrences interpolate trusted release/tag context rather than untrusted PR input.

findings.title: pull_request_target workflows check out PR-controlled refs
findings.description: Six workflows trigger on pull_request_target (which runs with the base repository's write-scoped token and secrets). At least devin-conflict-resolver.yml (checkout @ line 221, operating on pr.head_ref) and stale-pr-devin-completion.yml (checkout @ line 145) check out PR-controlled branches under that trigger, the classic pattern that can leak the privileged token / secrets to untrusted PR code.
findings.recommendation: Avoid checking out and executing untrusted PR code under pull_request_target; prefer the workflow_run pattern or pin to the base ref and gate any PR-code execution behind manual approval.
findings.demotionReason: devin-conflict-resolver.yml is gated by a maintainer-applied label (line 23) and several pull_request_target workflows only orchestrate/dispatch the real CI via head_sha (run-ci.yml) rather than executing PR code with secrets.

findings.title: docker-compose ships hardcoded default database credentials
findings.description: The compose database service hardcodes POSTGRES_USER=unicorn_user and POSTGRES_PASSWORD=magical_password (lines 20-21). If reused beyond local development, these well-known defaults expose the database.
findings.recommendation: Source database credentials from environment variables / secrets and document that the compose file is for local development only.
findings.demotionReason: docker-compose.yml is a local-development convenience stack (not the production deployment manifest) and the credentials are illustrative placeholders.

findings.title: Outbound webhooks are sent unsigned when no subscriber secret is configured
findings.description: createWebhookSignature returns "" when params.secret is falsy (line 350), and _sendPayload only sets the X-Cal-Signature-256 header when the signature is truthy (lines 369-370). A subscriber that did not configure a secret therefore receives an unsigned POST, so it cannot verify payload authenticity/integrity and may act on a spoofed delivery.
findings.recommendation: Warn or block on creation of webhook subscriptions without a secret, and document that unsigned delivery offers no authenticity guarantee.
findings.demotionReason: When a secret is present, payloads are signed with HMAC-SHA256 (packages/features/webhooks/lib/sendPayload.ts:349); the unsigned path is an opt-in of the subscriber, not a verification bypass on inbound traffic.

findings.title: Inbound Vercel webhook verification uses the deprecated HMAC-SHA1 construction
findings.description: VercelWebhookGuard computes crypto.createHmac("sha1", webhookSecret) (line 44) to verify the x-vercel-signature header. SHA-1 is deprecated for collision resistance, and although HMAC-SHA1 remains a sound MAC, the algorithm choice is a hygiene concern.
findings.recommendation: Where the provider supports it, migrate to HMAC-SHA256; otherwise document that SHA-1 is mandated by the Vercel signature contract.
findings.demotionReason: HMAC-SHA1 has no practical forgery against MAC usage, the comparison is constant-time via crypto.timingSafeEqual (apps/api/v2/src/vercel-webhook.guard.ts:53-56), and the SHA-1 format is dictated by Vercel's external webhook contract.

findings.title: Input validation is globally enforced in API v2 but only per-route in API v1
findings.description: API v2 installs a global ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }) (bootstrap.ts:71-83) that strips unknown properties on every DTO. API v1 instead relies on per-route Zod parsing, so any v1 handler that forgets to validate its body/query accepts arbitrary unvalidated input, creating an enforcement asymmetry across the two APIs.
findings.recommendation: Standardize a v1 validation wrapper (or shared schema-first handler factory) so body/query validation is structurally guaranteed, matching the v2 global pipe.
findings.demotionReason: Zod schemas are widely used across apps/api/v1/lib/validations and payloads are validated with safeParse at trust boundaries (e.g. packages/app-store/btcpayserver/api/webhook.ts:54), limiting the practical gap.

findings.title: Type-confusion surface from parsing untrusted JSON/structured input
findings.description: The Layer 3a inventory enumerates a large CWE-843 (type confusion) surface where untrusted input is parsed and consumed; without strict schema coercion at every boundary, mismatched types can bypass downstream assumptions.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every external input boundary uses strict schema validation/coercion (Zod/class-validator) before the value is used.
findings.demotionReason: The v2 ValidationPipe transforms and whitelists DTOs and v1 uses Zod safeParse at boundaries, so most parse sites already coerce types; residual risk is in any unguarded boundary.

findings.title: Parent-to-iframe postMessage uses a wildcard ('*') targetOrigin
findings.description: doInIframe posts commands to the embedded iframe with targetOrigin "*" (embed.ts:409-411), acknowledged by the in-code TODO at line 407. If the iframe is ever navigated to an unexpected origin, those command messages (method/arg) are delivered to that origin, leaking embed command context cross-origin.
findings.recommendation: Derive targetOrigin from the configured embed origin (__config.origin) and pass it explicitly instead of "*".
findings.demotionReason: The messages carry non-sensitive UI commands tagged originator:"CAL", and in practice the iframe is the operator's own cal.com origin; no credentials or tokens traverse this channel.

findings.title: Parent message listener fires SDK actions without validating event.origin
findings.description: The global window message handler (embed.ts:1597-1614) reads e.data and dispatches actionManager.fire(...) based solely on the message's fullType, without checking e.origin. Any frame/window able to post a well-formed message can trigger embed SDK actions in the host page.
findings.recommendation: Validate e.origin against the configured embed origin allowlist before processing inbound messages.
findings.demotionReason: Dispatched actions are client-side UI events (resize, link-ready, error surfacing) routed through namespaced actionManagers with no privileged/server-side effect, bounding the blast radius.

findings.title: API v1 accepts the API key via URL query parameter while v2 uses an Authorization header
findings.description: Legacy v1 reads the key from req.query.apiKey (verifyApiKey.ts:25,27 and rateLimitApiKey.ts:9), so secrets land in URLs and are routinely captured by access logs, proxies, and browser history. API v2 instead takes an Authorization: Bearer header, a divergence that weakens the v1 surface.
findings.recommendation: Accept the v1 key via Authorization header (deprecating the query parameter) to match v2 and avoid secret leakage through URL logging.
findings.demotionReason: Keys are SHA-256 hashed before lookup (verifyApiKey.ts:28) so logs never contain the stored secret form, and transport is HTTPS; the query-parameter form is retained for backward compatibility.

findings.title: Divergent enforcement models: per-route middleware (v1) vs global guards (v2)
findings.description: v2 enforces auth/validation/throttling globally (ValidationPipe + ~15 guard folders under apps/api/v2/src/modules/auth/guards), whereas v1 depends on each route opting into withMiddleware. The two surfaces can drift, so a protection present in v2 may be silently absent on the analogous v1 endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Document a parity matrix of controls across v1/v2 and converge toward default-enforced protection in v1.
findings.demotionReason: Both APIs implement authentication and rate limiting; the difference is enforcement mechanism, not absence of controls, and v1's shared middleware helper standardizes the chain.

findings.title: Rate-limiting algorithms differ between v1 (per-user) and v2 (per-credential/IP with DB limits)
findings.description: v1 throttles by numeric userId (rateLimitApiKey.ts:13) via checkRateLimitAndThrowError, while v2 throttles by SHA-256 hash of API key/access token/OAuth client (falling back to IP) with per-key DB-configured limits. The divergent identity and limit models make consistent quota enforcement across versions difficult to reason about.
findings.recommendation: Define a shared rate-limit policy/specification and align identifiers and default limits across v1 and v2.
findings.demotionReason: Both versions enforce rate limits and emit X-RateLimit-* headers, and @unkey/ratelimit underpins limiting; the divergence is an operational-consistency concern, not a missing control.

findings.title: Committed CRON_API_KEY default in .env.example guards 10+ sensitive cron routes
findings.description: The committed environment template sets CRON_API_KEY to a fixed 32-hex literal value (redacted here as 0cc0e6**REDACTED**) that authorizes 10+ App Router cron endpoints (e.g. apps/web/app/api/cron/downgradeUsers, /credentials, /changeTimeZone, /webhookTriggers). Because the value is public in the repository, any deployment that does not override it exposes privileged maintenance operations to anyone who replays the well-known key.
findings.recommendation: Remove the literal value from the committed template (leave CRON_API_KEY= blank like NEXTAUTH_SECRET), require operators to generate a unique key, and rotate any environment that adopted the default.
findings.demotionReason: The value lives in .env.example (a template), not in a committed live .env, and production deployments are expected to set their own CRON_API_KEY; the cron handlers do enforce the key before acting.

findings.title: Cron endpoint authorization uses a non-constant-time comparison and accepts the key via query string
findings.description: Representative cron handlers read the secret as request.headers.get("authorization") || searchParams.get("apiKey") (line 14) and authorize with a plain process.env.CRON_API_KEY !== apiKey comparison (line 16). The query-parameter acceptance leaks the secret into URL logs, and the !== comparison is not constant-time, exposing a timing side-channel on the secret.
findings.recommendation: Compare the cron secret with crypto.timingSafeEqual and accept it only via the Authorization header (drop the apiKey query parameter).
findings.demotionReason: The cron secret is a high-entropy 32-hex token, making a network-observable timing attack impractical, and transport is HTTPS; the comparison gates a non-interactive maintenance endpoint rather than user auth.

findings.title: Multiple dangerouslySetInnerHTML usages create a React XSS sink surface
findings.description: Semgrep identifies nine dangerouslySetInnerHTML usages across apps/web (e.g. EventTypeDescription.tsx:63, slug-view.tsx:71, team-view.tsx:161, users-public-view.tsx:108). Each is a potential stored/reflected XSS sink if the injected HTML derives from user-controllable content without robust sanitization.
findings.recommendation: Audit each usage to confirm the HTML is constant or sanitized (e.g. DOMPurify) and replace with safe rendering where the source is user-controlled.
findings.demotionReason: React escapes all default output and these are a small, enumerable set of intentional rich-text/markdown render points typically fed sanitized or trusted content; this is a surface to verify, not a confirmed injection.
findings.corroboration: Semgrep typescript.react.security.audit.react-dangerouslysetinnerhtml (9 hits) + Layer 3a sink-inventory CWE-79 (53 hits)

summary.note: Layer 1 findings are architectural and advisory; each carries a demotionReason crediting the compensating controls catalogued in AAP section 0.2.3. The gate verdict is computed downstream in findings-merged.json across all layers.
